doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Welk's rise to television and the Tiger Rag floor routine
summary: Welk's territory band history and move to national TV; Havens's lying-down Tiger Rag solo wins him the job, which lasts twenty-two years.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Excuse me, was this pre-TV? Was he traveling the country like other bands?

Lawrence was known as a territory band. There were hundreds of territory type bands that just played engagements in hotels and just like a circuit, like all the bands were doing. Lawrence started out in the midwest, from the Dakotas. And in 1948 he migrated with his band to the west coast. And he began playing at the Aragon Ballroom in Santa Monica. Well through good management he landed a job with his orchestra on a local television, in 1954 I think it was. In ‘55 the Chrysler Company, the Dodge people, picked him as a replacement for “The Jackie Gleason Show” on television. So after years of local television, he worked his way to a national show. Well from that point on his popularity just grew by leaps and bounds. And he found himself able to sort of look around and get the cream of the crop through all existing musicians. So he’d heard me play. See I had a specialty that I started doing with Al Hirt, and that was somebody asked me to play a solo on “Tiger Rag.” Well it was a real fast number and somebody came in and said, “Well you know there’s a trombone player down the street that plays Tiger Rag, can you do that?” This was just a customer. And I said, “Well I don’t do that as a solo but I could try.” And I didn’t know what the other fellow did, I just — well he must be doing something special. So I just started acting like a clown. You know I’d play and I would lay on the floor, and move the slide with my foot and kind of like a circus act. And this fellow just went crazy over what I did, along with the rest of the audience. And I thought well that’s the end of that, I won’t have to do that anymore, hopefully. The next night a bunch of people came in and says, “We saw you do this thing where you lay on the floor,” and you know this became a nightly routine and I had to keep doing it and keep doing it, and it has become a trademark with me ever since. And this is what caught Mr. Welk’s eye. He saw me do that one night and he said, “Anybody that can do that,” (playing the trombone laying on his back and moving the slide with his foot) “anybody
that can do that should be on my show.” So that was really singularly responsible for getting me the job, just that one song.
But of course he did like my playing other than that. But that started my career with the champagne music. And it lasted twenty-two years.

And I thought I might last about six months, being a jazz player. But I did find out that Mr. Welk loved jazz music and he had said to me before that he sometimes wished that he had started a jazz band because he liked it so well.
